reason: Tepals can ascend, spread or arch. The examples are orientation.
Rhizoid surface can be papillose or smooth.
Hyaline (translucent) peristome teeth are an optical property. A rule could map hyaline to a more specific transparency term.
Herbaceous versus membranous tepal texture is a standard contrast.
'Roots few' counts roots, so the bearer is the stem, node or plant and not a single root. Wrong bearer.
A leaf apex can be twisted or contorted.
Mericarps can be keeled or carinate. The examples are correct.
Leaflet surfaces can be sticky or glutinous.
The examples give the shape of the ray flower lamina (ligule), so 2-D shape fits.
'Ovoid' is a 3-D shape and PATO ovate is a 2-D outline. Wrong reading. Use the ovoid class pending in pato#627.
Pedicels and peduncles can be branched.
Stipules can be succulent. A negated 'not succulent' needs the negation rule.
Bracteoles can be shiny or glossy.
Chestnut or brown perianth segments are a colour, so red brown fits.
The sinus (or the base) is open, not the lamina. Wrong bearer. The part would need to be the sinus.
The examples say veins run perpendicular to the midrib. The bearer is the vein, not the lamina.
A small or minute elaiosome is a size quality.
A lobe can be flattened.
The examples describe a tube (hypanthium or calyx tube) as obconic. This is a plausible shape. The class has no label here, so check the bearer.
'Filiferous' means bearing threads. That is possession of parts, not a filamentous shape of the margin. Wrong reading.
Variegated, bicolored or tigrées stems are multi-coloured.
Pale versus bright flower colour is saturation.
A replum can be flattened. This is a diagnostic character in Brassicaceae.
The number of oil glands is a count.
'Short-stalked' describes the stalk, not the sporangium length. Wrong part.
Hyaline or transparent septa are meaningful. The 'large hyaline areas' example is partial and needs care.
A crown can be membranous or callous. These are texture terms.
A petal apex can be recurved.
Lineate or striated surfaces are meaningful. Check that the parallel veins example is not a venation pattern.
Secondary veins can be convex, that is, raised.
'To 2 cm wide' is a measurement, not an 'increased width' quality. Wrong reading. Use the measured width rule.
The examples describe cone scale apophyses and umbos, not the sporangium base. Wrong part.
Solitary or whorled is an arrangement of cones.
Shoots can be ascending.
Suberect leaf blades are common in bryophyte and fern descriptions.
Exothecium surface can be scabrous or papillate.
Leaflets can be soft to the touch.
A weak blade is meaningful. The 'weak veins' example belongs to the vein, so it needs checking.
Abaxial surfaces can be hispid. The examples are annotated correctly.
Throat length is a valid length. The 'longa' example is a typo but still a length.
Spinulose tepal margins or surfaces exist, for example in Juncaceae and Cyperaceae.
Diameter is a valid quality, and 'de diam.' is a diameter.
Hyaline sporophyll margins or bodies are meaningful.
An apex can be truncate.
Flower buds can be clavate.
Achenes can be erect.
Stamens or filaments can be ascending.
Bracts can be scaly or lepidote.
Pale spores are a low-saturation colour.
Epicalyx bracts or lobes can be filiform.
A margin can be thickened.
The examples say 'inside hairy', which is the inner surface of another organ (such as a tube or sheath), not the short shoot. A rule would need to read the part named in the sentence.
The number of samaras is a count.
Lodicules can be transparent.
Pedicels can be oblique upward.
Seeds can bear bristles. The examples are correct.
Long organs such as a beak or stolon are an increased length. Plain measurements like '1–3 mm long' need the measured length rule.
Lobes can be triangular or deltoid.
Margins can be erose.
Lateral veins can be flattened.
